payload.name: cepstral-normalization
payload.scope: A human-made normalization procedure applied to cepstral coefficients to remove artifacts from recording conditions and channel effects, making coefficients comparable across speakers and sessions.

definition.body: Cepstral normalization is a preprocessing procedure that removes additive and multiplicative distortions from cepstral coefficients to improve robustness across speakers, microphones, and recording conditions. The two standard methods are: (1) cepstral mean normalization (CMN), which subtracts the per-coefficient mean across an utterance or session, removing static bias; (2) cepstral variance normalization (CVN), which further divides by the per-coefficient standard deviation to equalize dynamic range. Parameters: (1) the normalization scope — utterance-level, session-level, or global; (2) the coefficient indices included (typically excluding c[0] which encodes energy); (3) whether mean and variance are computed separately per coefficient or jointly. Persistence mechanism: implemented as a standard preprocessing step in speech recognition front-ends (HTK, Kaldi, librosa), specified in NIST speaker recognition evaluations, and used in all major AISI benchmark pipelines. e.g.: Kaldi's cmn() function applied to MFCC features before GMM-HMM decoding; HTK's cepstral mean normalization in the WSJ speech recognition front-end; NIST speaker recognition evaluation pre-processing of MFCC with utterance-level CMN | not: cepstral-mean-normalization; cepstral-mean-variance-normalization [formal: normalized cepstrum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cross-phase-spectrum
payload.scope: Made so that the phase relationship between two signals can be measured and used separately from the magnitudes of their cross-spectral density, for delay estimation, phase-based coupling analysis, and phase consistency checks in system identification.

definition.body: The cross-phase spectrum is a human-made bivariate spectral measure that quantifies the phase difference between two signals at each frequency, defined as the argument of their cross-spectral density: cross-phase(f) = arg S_xy(f), where S_xy(f) is the cross-spectral density of the two signals. It separates the phase part of the cross-spectral density from its magnitude part, so that a change in relative phase between the signals is visible without being masked by a change in the magnitude of the cross-spectrum. Unlike the cross-spectrum (the raw complex conjugate product) or the cross-spectral density (which carries both magnitude and phase), the cross-phase spectrum carries only the phase angle, normalized to the principal value range -pi to pi. Unlike the phase spectrum of a single signal (arg X(f)), it is bivariate: it compares the phases of two signals against each other, not the phase of one signal against its own zero reference. Parameters: (1) the two signals being compared, (2) the spectral estimation method (direct periodogram, Welch averaged, or multitaper), (3) the averaging window length, which stabilizes the phase estimate against noise since a single-estimate cross-phase is unreliable in low signal-to-noise regions. Persistence mechanism: standardized in vibration testing and system identification protocols where the phase of the transfer function is read from the cross-phase, maintained in spectral analysis libraries (MATLAB cpsd, SciPy csd), and used in neuroscience for phase-amplitude and phase-phase coupling between signals, in acoustics for time-delay estimation between microphone or station pairs, and in seismology for inter-station phase-delay estimation. e.g.: cross-phase of a vibration transfer function read from the cpsd output in ANSI S1.11 vibration testing; inter-station cross-phase in seismological phase-delay estimation between two recording stations; phase-phase coupling between EEG and fMRI signals in AFNI fMRI preprocessing | not: cross-spectrum (the raw complex conjugate product carrying magnitude and phase); phase-spectrum (the univariate arg X(f) of one signal); coherence-function (a magnitude ratio, not a phase angle) [formal: phasium inter-signale spectrum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.note: DEPENDS_ON (Laws 8, 8a): removal test. The cross-phase spectrum is defined as arg S_xy(f): the phase angle IS the argument of the cross-spectral density. payload.name: frequency-domain
payload.scope: Made so that a signal can be analyzed, specified, and measured by the amplitudes and phases of its frequency components instead of by its waveform, giving the discipline a boundary - the frequency-versus-time split - that its curricula, standards, and instruments keep in daily use.

definition.body: The frequency-domain is the human-made representational map in which a signal is described by the amplitudes and phases of its frequency components rather than by its instantaneous values in time. Signal processing and its users in communications, acoustics, and seismology draw the map's boundary: it takes in descriptions that express a signal by its frequency content - spectra, power-spectral densities, transfer functions, spectrograms - and leaves out descriptions of the signal's moment-by-moment values; the same discipline draws neighboring maps with different lines (the cepstral domain inverts the log-magnitude spectrum, the wavelet map joins time and frequency in one plane). The map's parameters are the transform convention used (continuous or discrete Fourier, windowed STFT), the axis convention (Hz or rad/s), and the representation form (magnitude, phase, power, complex). The map persists in the textbooks and curricula that teach the frequency-versus-time split, in the standards that specify frequency measurements (ANSI S1.11 vibration, ISO 16063 accelerometer calibration), in the instruments that display it (spectrum analyzers, FFT software), and in the shared vocabulary - spectrum, bandwidth, harmonic, resonance - that keeps the split in everyday use. e.g.: the frequency axis of an STFT spectrogram computed in MATLAB spectrogram; the frequency-response plot (magnitude and phase) of an LTI system in Oppenheim and Schafer DSP; the power-spectral-density plot of a vibration signal per ANSI S1.11 | not: the time-domain waveform of the same signal (the time map, not the frequency map); the cepstral domain (a map of the log-magnitude spectrum, a different representational space) [formal: regio frequentiae | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The time-domain is the human-made representational map in which a signal is described by its values at successive instants rather than by the amplitudes and phases of its frequency components. Signal processing and its users in communications, acoustics, and seismology draw the map's boundary: it takes in descriptions that give the signal's instantaneous or sampled values over time - waveforms, sampled sequences, impulse responses - and leaves out descriptions that express the same signal by its frequency content; the same discipline draws the neighboring frequency-domain map across exactly this line (and the wavelet map joins the two in one plane). payload.name: inverse-short-time-fourier-transform
payload.scope: A human-made signal-processing procedure that reconstructs a time-domain signal from a short-time Fourier (STFT) decomposition by frame-wise inverse transform and overlap-and-add synthesis.

definition.body: The inverse short-time Fourier transform (ISTFT) is a signal-processing procedure that reconstructs a time-domain signal from a short-time Fourier representation. Given a complex-valued STFT matrix (the time–frequency decomposition of a signal), the ISTFT applies the inverse Fourier transform to each time frame, then sums the reconstructed segments with overlap-and-add to recover the original signal. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic — defined by frame-wise IDFT and weighted overlap-add synthesis, implementable in software or hardware. e.g.: the librosa.istft function in the librosa Python library; the MATLAB istft function in Signal Processing Toolbox; the inverse-STFT step in the Griffin-Lim phase-reconstruction algorithm | not: the time-domain waveform of the original signal [formal: inversa transformatio Fourier temporis brevi | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: inverse-discrete-fourier-transform
payload.scope: Made so that a processed frequency representation can be returned to the time domain: the reciprocal step that closes the DFT pair and makes spectral processing reversible.

definition.body: The inverse discrete Fourier transform (IDFT) is a mathematical algorithm that reconstructs a finite sequence of N time-domain samples from a finite sequence of N frequency-domain complex coefficients. It computes x[n] = (1/N) * sum_{k=0}^{N-1} X[k] * exp(2*pi*i*k*n/N) for n = 0,...,N-1 — the reciprocal kernel of the DFT, with the 1/N normalization that makes the pair exact: applying the DFT then the IDFT returns the original sequence up to numerical error, and via the FFT the inverse is the same recursion with the kernel conjugated. Parameters: length N, the coefficient sequence X[k], the normalization convention (1/N on the inverse, or symmetric 1/sqrt(N) on both directions), and the numerical precision of the complex arithmetic. Persistence mechanism: a standardized algorithm encoded in every major numerical library and taught as the synthesis half of the transform pair; it is the named frame-wise step of the inverse STFT and of overlap-add synthesis. e.g.: numpy.fft.ifft in the NumPy library; the MATLAB ifft function in the Signal Processing Toolbox; the frame-wise inverse-DFT step of the Griffin-Lim algorithm | not: the inverse STFT on a time-frequency matrix, which adds overlap-add; the continuous inverse Fourier integral [formal: inversa transformatio Fourier discreta | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: Made so that a processed frequency representation can be returned to the time domain: the reciprocal step that closes the DFT pair and makes spectral processing reversible.

definition.body: The inverse discrete Fourier transform (IDFT) is a mathematical algorithm that reconstructs a finite sequence of N time-domain samples from a finite sequence of N frequency-domain complex coefficients. It computes x[n] = (1/N) * sum_{k=0}^{N-1} X[k] * exp(2*pi*i*k*n/N) for n = 0,...,N-1 — the reciprocal kernel of the DFT, with the 1/N normalization that makes the pair exact: applying the DFT then the IDFT returns the original sequence up to numerical error, and via the FFT the inverse is the same recursion with the kernel conjugated. Parameters: length N, the coefficient sequence X[k], the normalization convention (1/N on the inverse, or symmetric 1/sqrt(N) on both directions), and the numerical precision of the complex arithmetic. Persistence mechanism: a standardized algorithm encoded in every major numerical library and taught as the synthesis half of the transform pair; it is the named frame-wise step of the inverse STFT and of overlap-add synthesis. e.g.: numpy.fft.ifft in the NumPy library; the MATLAB ifft function in the Signal Processing Toolbox; the frame-wise inverse-DFT step of the Griffin-Lim algorithm | not: the inverse STFT on a time-frequency matrix, which adds overlap-add; the continuous inverse Fourier integral [formal: inversa transformatio Fourier discreta | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: phase-delay
payload.scope: A human-made analytical measure of the time delay experienced by the phase of an individual frequency component as it passes through a system, used to characterize phase linearity in filter design and communications.

definition.body: Phase-delay is the time delay experienced by the phase of an individual frequency component as it passes through a system. It is defined as tau_p(omega) = -phi(omega)/omega, where phi(omega) is the phase response at angular frequency omega and the negative sign ensures that a positive phase lag yields a positive delay. Unlike group-delay (the envelope delay -dphi/domega), phase-delay tracks the absolute time offset of each frequency component's zero crossings. A system with constant phase-delay across all frequencies produces no phase distortion, since every frequency component is shifted by the same amount of time, preserving waveform shape. Parameters: (1) the phase response phi(omega), (2) angular frequency omega, (3) the convention for unwrapped phase (removing 2pi ambiguities). Persistence mechanism: encoded in filter design theory, network analysis, and communications systems where phase linearity is a design criterion. e.g.: the phase delay of a first-order RC low-pass filter; the phase-delay equalizer in audio crossover networks; dispersion-compensated fiber-optic link phase response | not: group-delay; phase shift; phase spectrum [formal: tarditas phasis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.name: magnitude-response
payload.scope: A human-made analytical measure separating the amplitude branch of a system's frequency response so that designers can specify, plot, and correct a system's gain behavior across frequency - bandwidth, ripple, roll-off - independently of its phase.

definition.body: The magnitude-response is the amplitude branch of a linear system's complex frequency response: the function |H(f)| that assigns to each frequency f the modulus of the complex frequency response H(f) = |H(f)|·e^(jφ(f)), i.e., the ratio of steady-state output amplitude to input amplitude at that frequency. Parameters: (1) the frequency variable, spanning DC to the system's bandwidth; (2) the expression convention - dimensionless linear ratio or 20·log10(|H|) decibels; (3) the reference level against which decibels are taken. Unlike gain (a single ratio at one operating point) it is a function across frequency, and unlike the magnitude-spectrum (the modulus of a particular signal's spectral coefficients) it is a property of the system, not of a signal. Persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard plot and specification of filter and amplifier design - the magnitude axis of the Bode plot (Hendrik Bode, 1945), network-analyzer measurements, and datasheet gain specifications. e.g.: the passband ripple and stopband attenuation of a Butterworth low-pass filter; the gain curve of a Class-A audio power amplifier on its datasheet; the modulus trace of a measurement channel's transfer function on a vector network analyzer | not: gain; magnitude-spectrum; phase-response [formal: magnitudo responsus | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: bode-plot
payload.scope: To read a system's stability margins, bandwidth, and phase behavior directly from a straight-line-approximable log-log rendering of its frequency response, so designers can assess and correct phase and gain without solving the closed-loop equations.

definition.body: The bode-plot is a graphical rendering of a linear system's frequency response as a pair of curves on a logarithmic frequency axis: the magnitude curve (in decibels) and the phase curve (in degrees or radians), both plotted against log frequency. Parameters: (1) the frequency axis on a logarithmic scale, in decades; (2) the magnitude axis in decibels (20·log10); (3) the phase axis in degrees or radians on a linear scale; (4) the asymptotic (break-frequency) approximation, where each pole or zero contributes a straight-line segment of slope plus or minus 20·n dB per decade to the magnitude and plus or minus 45 degrees per decade to the phase, meeting at its corner frequency. Persistence mechanism: maintained as the standard hand-analysis and design tool of feedback control and filter design - Bode's 1945 paper 'Relation between magnitude and phase in feedback systems' and the control-textbook tradition that follows it - used to read the gain margin and phase margin at the gain-crossover and phase-crossover frequencies and to correct a system's phase behavior by adding lead or lag compensation. e.g.: the asymptotic straight-line Bode plot of a second-order low-pass filter in Ogata's Modern Control Engineering; the gain- and phase-margin reading of an open-loop transfer function at the gain-crossover frequency; the Bode plot of a single-pole RC low-pass filter as the worked straight-line example in Bode's 1945 paper | not: nyquist-plot (the polar plot of the same complex response, not log-log); root-locus (the closed-loop pole path as gain varies, not the frequency response); gain-margin (the scalar quantity read off the plot, not the plot itself) [formal: descriptio responsus | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

Evaluating a linear system's complex response H(omega) to sinusoidal inputs predates the plot: the jw-axis treatment runs through 1920s-30s network analysis, and Nyquist's 1932 stability criterion already worked with the system's gain and phase characteristics.
